subject: Civil Engineering
title: Construction Safety Management
description: A quick win: understand Construction Safety Management.

hook.text: Construction kills more workers than any other industry — falls, struck-by, and trenching collapses.

buildup.text: OSHA's Fatal Four — falls, struck-by, electrocution, caught-between — cause 60% of deaths.

discovery.text: Safety plans identify hazards and controls before work starts — prevention, not reaction.

twist.text: Near-miss reporting catches dangers before injuries — sites that track near-misses have fewer accidents.

climax.text: The construction fatality rate dropped 65% since 1970 — OSHA regulations and culture change saved lives.

punchline.text: Every safety rule was written after someone got hurt. Prevention is the only way.

quiz.question: What are OSHA's Fatal Four causes of construction deaths?
options: Fire, flooding, gas leaks, and structural collapse
Falls, struck-by objects, electrocution, and caught-between hazards
Heat stroke, dehydration, chemical exposure, and noise

details.summary: Construction safety management implements systematic programs to prevent worker injuries and fatalities on job sites. Programs include hazard identification, safety training, personal protective equipment requirements, fall protection systems, excavation safety protocols.
details.whyItMatters: Construction has one of the highest fatality rates of any industry. Falls, struck-by incidents, electrocution, and caught-in hazards account for over 60% of construction deaths each year.
takeaways: Falls are the leading cause of construction fatalities worldwide
Safety programs reduce injury rates by 50 to 80% when properly implemented
Near-miss reporting identifies hazards before they cause actual injuries

faq.question: What are the construction industry's fatal four hazards?
faq.answer: The fatal four are falls from heights, struck-by-object incidents when materials or equipment hit workers, electrocution from contact with power lines or unprotected wiring, and caught-in-between hazards where workers are trapped by collapsing materials or equipment.

faq.question: How do safety programs measure their effectiveness?
faq.answer: Total Recordable Incident Rate (TRIR) tracks injuries per 200,000 work hours. Experience Modification Rate (EMR) compares a company's injury record against industry average.
